name: Time-series cross-validation, purging and embargo. Core: Bergmeir & Benitez (2012), 'On the use of cross-validation for time series predictor evaluation' (Information Sciences 191:192-213), and Lopez de Prado (2018), 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning' (Wiley), ch. 7 'Cross-Validation in Finance' (purged k-fold + embargo) and ch. 12 (combinatorial purged CV, CPCV). Companions: Bergmeir, Hyndman & Koo (2018), 'A note on the validity of cross-validation for evaluating autoregressive time series prediction' (CSDA 120:70-83); Cerqueira, Torgo & Mozetic (2020), 'Evaluating time series forecasting models: an empirical study on performance estimation methods' (Machine Learning 109:1997-2028); Tashman (2000), 'Out-of-sample tests of forecasting accuracy: an analysis and review' (IJF 16(4):437-450); Racine (2000), hv-block CV (J. Econometrics); Hewamalage, Ackermann & Bergmeir (2023), 'Forecast evaluation for data scientists: common pitfalls and best practices' (DMKD 37(2):788-832); Roberts et al. (2017), CV for temporal/spatial structure (Ecography).
type: method family (evaluation protocol: walk-forward / rolling-origin evaluation, blocked and hv-block CV, purging of overlapping labels at cut-offs, embargo after test folds, CPCV)
url: Bergmeir & Benitez 2012: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2011.12.028 (record: https://research.monash.edu/en/publications/on-the-use-of-cross-validation-for-time-series-predictor-evaluati/) ; Lopez de Prado 2018 (book, Wiley, ISBN 978-1-119-48208-6 [uncertain]) - no open full text; implementations: https://temporalcv.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/cv_financial.html , https://mizarlabs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/mizarlabs.model.html , https://skfolio.org/_modules/skfolio/model_selection/_combinatorial.html , https://fynance.readthedocs.io/en/latest/generated/fynance.data.combinatorial_purged_cv.html ; Bergmeir, Hyndman & Koo 2018: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csda.2017.11.003 (working paper: https://ideas.repec.org/p/msh/ebswps/2015-10.html ; R implementation forecast::CVar https://pkg.robjhyndman.com/forecast/reference/CVar.html) ; Cerqueira et al. 2020: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-020-05910-7 (preprint https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.11744) ; Tashman 2000: https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/intfor/v16y2000i4p437-450.html ; Hewamalage et al. 2023: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9718476 (arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.10716) ; scikit-learn TimeSeriesSplit(gap=): https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit.html

Cerqueira et al.: 2020 (arXiv 2019). Tashman: 2000. Racine: 2000. Hewamalage et al.: 2023 (arXiv 2022). scikit-learn TimeSeriesSplit gap/test_size: added in v0.24 (Dec 2020). Retrieved 2026-10-17.
authors: Christoph Bergmeir, Jose M. Benitez (Univ. Granada); Marcos Lopez de Prado; Christoph Bergmeir, Rob J. Hyndman, Bonsoo Koo (Monash); Vitor Cerqueira, Luis Torgo, Igor Mozetic; Leonard J. Tashman; Jeff Racine; Hansika Hewamalage, Klaus Ackermann, Christoph Bergmeir; David R. Roberts et al.
popularity: Semantic Scholar citation counts (retrieved 2026-10-17): Bergmeir & Benitez 2012 = 1,311; Bergmeir, Hyndman & Koo 2018 = 716; Cerqueira et al. 2020 = 517; Racine 2000 hv-block = 233; Roberts et al. 2017 = 3,202. Lopez de Prado 2018 (AFML) is the standard finance-ML reference for purging/embargo; several thousand Google Scholar citations [uncertain: count not retrieved, Semantic Scholar rate-limited]. Purged k-fold / CPCV are implemented in many open libraries (mlfinlab, now closed-source; temporalcv; skfolio; mizarlabs; fynance).
peer_review_status: peer-reviewed: Bergmeir & Benitez 2012 (Information Sciences), Bergmeir et al. 2018 (CSDA), Cerqueira et al. 2020 (Machine Learning), Tashman 2000 (IJF), Racine 2000 (J. Econometrics), Hewamalage et al. 2023 (DMKD), Roberts et al. 2017 (Ecography). Lopez de Prado 2018 is a practitioner book (publisher-edited, not journal peer review); purging/embargo is argued conceptually, not validated in a controlled empirical study in the book [uncertain].
target_type: Not applicable (method literature). Relevance to target type: purging is defined on the LABEL interval [t0, t1] of each row. For our onset target y(t) = 1 if a new alert starts in (t, t+H], the label interval is (t, t+H], so the purge width equals H. A state target ('under alert at t+H') would have the same label interval but much stronger serial dependence between neighbouring rows, which makes leakage through adjacent rows (the embargo argument) more damaging; the at-risk mask removes most of that persistence.
target_definition: Generic: each observation i has features known at t_i,0 and a label determined by outcomes up to t_i,1 (Lopez de Prado's 't1' series). Bergmeir & Benitez use autoregressive embeddings: predict x_t from (x_{t-1}, ..., x_{t-p}), one-step horizon. For us: t_i,0 = t (hour start, UTC), t_i,1 = t + H, H = 1 default (H = 3 tested in M3b).
spatial_unit: Not applicable (single series in Bergmeir/Cerqueira; single asset in Lopez de Prado). Roberts et al. 2017 extend blocking to spatial/hierarchical structure. For us: a panel of 24 oblast-level units sharing one clock; split blocks must contain all 24 units for the same hours.
at_risk_masking: Not applicable in the papers. Interaction with our protocol: the masked (already-under-alert) rows are dropped AFTER purging; a purged row and a masked row are counted separately in src/evaluate.py eligibility() (exclusive order purge -> masked -> y_nan -> feature_nan), so the purge count is reported honestly even when the row would also be masked.
data_sources: Bergmeir & Benitez 2012: synthetic AR-type series plus real-world series; six model-selection procedures (CV-based and last-block hold-out) applied to four ML / regression techniques [uncertain: exact procedure names and datasets not verified from full text]. Bergmeir et al. 2018: simulation study plus a real-world example. Cerqueira et al. 2020: 174 real-world series plus three synthetic series. Lopez de Prado 2018: financial bar data (prices, triple-barrier labels), conceptual examples.
preprocessing: Not applicable directly. Method rules relevant to preprocessing (Hewamalage et al. 2023, Sec. 3): normalising, smoothing or decomposing the full series before splitting leaks the future; transformations and summary features must be fit on each training window only or recomputed over the input window; global models across unaligned series can leak when one series carries future information about another. These match CLAUDE.md 'Forbidden: centered windows, scalers/encoders fit on full data, any statistic computed over the test period'.
known_label_artefacts: Not applicable to air alerts. The method-level 'artefact' is overlapping labels: when labels span several rows (H > 1, or Lopez de Prado's triple-barrier labels lasting days), neighbouring rows share outcomes. Consequences: (1) leakage across a cut-off unless purged; (2) the effective sample size is smaller than the row count, which Lopez de Prado handles with average-uniqueness sample weights and the sequential bootstrap (AFML ch. 4) [uncertain: chapter number from memory]. For us: with H = 1 on an hourly grid, labels (t, t+1] do not overlap, so neither problem arises; with H = 3 each onset appears in up to 3 consecutive labels.
model_family: Evaluation protocols, not models. (1) Walk-forward / rolling-origin evaluation (Tashman 2000): successive forecast origins, either updating or recalibrating the model, fixed or expanding windows, multiple test periods. (2) Blocked K-fold CV (Bergmeir & Benitez 2012): contiguous folds instead of random ones; recommended as standard for (stationary) series. (3) h-block / hv-block CV (Burman, Chow & Nolan 1994; Racine 2000): remove h observations on each side of the test block from training; v controls the test block size. Bergmeir et al. 2018 call a lag-based variant 'non-dependent CV'. (4) Purged K-fold (Lopez de Prado 2018, ch. 7): remove from training every observation whose label interval [t0_i, t1_i] overlaps the label interval of any test observation; with test after train this reduces to dropping training rows with t1_i > test start. (5) Embargo: additionally drop training observations that come immediately AFTER a test fold (h observations, with h of about 0.01 T suggested as often sufficient [uncertain: exact wording and whether T is the full sample]); needed only when training data follows test data (k-fold), because serially correlated features right after the test fold still carry test information. (6) CPCV (AFML ch. 12): split into N groups, test on every combination of k groups, purge+embargo each split; C(N, k) splits recombine into (k/N) C(N, k) = C(N-1, k-1) backtest paths (e.g. N = 6, k = 2: 15 splits, 5 paths), giving a distribution of out-of-sample performance rather than one path. (7) scikit-learn TimeSeriesSplit(gap=g) drops g SAMPLES (rows, not time units) from the end of each training set before the test set.
features: Not applicable (no forecasting features). Key distinction: purging and embargo act on LABEL overlap, not on feature look-back. A test-row feature that looks back into the training period (e.g. our onsets_last_7d at the first test hour) is legitimate, because that information is known at t. Feature-side leakage (a feature reading data after t) is not fixed by any split scheme; it needs causal construction plus a truncation test (our tests/test_leakage.py with its negative control).
external_feature_timing: Not applicable. General rule from Hewamalage et al. 2023: summary statistics that will not be available at forecast time (e.g. full-day aggregates used for a next-day forecast) create a horizon mismatch; the label-maturity analogue for any rolling statistic built from labels is that a label for row s becomes known only at s + H.
ablation_design: Cerqueira et al. 2020 and Tashman 2000 favour repeated out-of-sample evaluation over several origins for model/feature selection on non-stationary data. Feature or model comparisons must use identical rows per fold (our M7 block_acceptance does this: every candidate feature is known on the same eligible rows; 4 inner folds with cut-offs 2025-07-01, 2025-10-01, 2026-01-01, 2026-04-01, 14-day early-stopping slices and 8-week scoring windows, all before validation).
split_scheme: Recommendations by condition: (a) stationary series, pure AR model with uncorrelated residuals: standard or blocked K-fold CV is valid and uses data more efficiently (Bergmeir et al. 2018; check residual autocorrelation with Ljung-Box first, as forecast::CVar does). (b) Non-stationary real-world series: out-of-sample methods that preserve temporal order, especially hold-out repeated over several test periods, give the most accurate performance estimates (Cerqueira et al. 2020); rolling-origin is preferred whenever non-stationarity is present, and abrupt structural breaks in the unseen future cannot be handled by any scheme (Hewamalage et al. 2023). (c) Overlapping labels or serially correlated features with K-fold: purge plus embargo (Lopez de Prado 2018). (d) Walk-forward with train strictly before test: purging at the cut-off is required when H > 1 step; embargo is unnecessary because no training data lies after the test block.
metrics: Protocol papers, metric-agnostic. Bergmeir & Benitez 2012 and Cerqueira et al. 2020 measure how well each CV/hold-out estimate approximates the true out-of-sample error (estimation bias/accuracy) and model-selection robustness [uncertain: exact error measures not verified]. Lopez de Prado uses CV scores (e.g. negative log loss, accuracy) and, for CPCV, distributions of Sharpe ratios across paths. Hewamalage et al. 2023 discuss DM, Wilcoxon signed-rank and Giacomini-White tests, with Bonferroni-type corrections for multiple comparisons.
unit_of_metric: Single series (pooled) in the papers. For panels, Roberts et al. 2017 stress blocking on the dependence structure; for us metrics are pooled and per unit/group, but the SPLIT is always by date over all 24 units together.
baseline_strength: Hewamalage et al. 2023: always compare with the naive (no-change) forecast and, for seasonal data, the seasonal naive; in their leakage experiment a leaky setup made a random-walk forecast appear to beat the naive model (p of about 0.067), while the non-leaky version was significantly worse. Our analogue: the rolling recent-rate baseline (D-021) is the naive bar, and it must itself obey label maturity (s <= t - H).
calibration: Not addressed. Implication: any calibration map must be fitted on a slice that is purged with respect to the scored slice (our D-021: fitted on validation, which ends with t + H <= test start, and applied to the same frozen model).
calibration_under_drift: Indirect. Cerqueira et al. 2020 and Hewamalage et al. 2023 show that CV with future data in training underestimates error under non-stationarity; rolling-origin and repeated hold-out reveal drift that a single random split hides. Our measured base-rate shift (train 0.0903 vs validation 0.1179, D-025) is exactly the case where K-fold or blocked CV with future training data would be optimistic.
uncertainty_of_gain: Lopez de Prado: a single walk-forward path gives one performance number and is easy to overfit; CPCV gives a distribution across paths; related work (Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado & Zhu, 'The probability of backtest overfitting', J. Computational Finance 2017) quantifies selection bias from trying many variants [uncertain: citation details from memory]. Hewamalage et al. 2023: DM / Wilcoxon / Giacomini-White tests, corrected for multiple comparisons. For overlapping labels, the effective sample size must account for overlap (uniqueness weights). For us: week-block bootstrap (D-013) handles serial and cross-sectional dependence; with only 6 test weeks the CI is indicative.
regime_coverage: Not applicable (no alert data). General result: under regime change, CV schemes that train on data after the test fold leak the future regime level; only forward-only evaluation reflects deployment. Our test window (27 Jul - 7 Sep 2026) lies after the Jan-2025 drone surge and the 2025 raion reform; the Sep-2026 yellow/red reform is evaluated separately (D-015), and no CV scheme makes a pre-reform test informative about a post-reform regime.
leakage_handling: Mechanisms documented in the literature: (1) Purging: drop training rows whose label window overlaps any test label window; for train-before-test this is 'keep a training row iff t + H <= cut-off'. (2) Embargo: drop training rows right after a test fold (only when training follows testing). (3) hv-block/non-dependent CV: drop rows within the lag/dependence distance of the test block. (4) Causal preprocessing: fit transformations per training window (Hewamalage et al.). (5) Row-index splitting pitfalls: scikit-learn TimeSeriesSplit gap counts rows; on a stacked panel (24 rows per hour) a row-index split can cut through an hour and put same-hour rows of other oblasts (strongly correlated in mass attacks) on both sides. What our project does (verified in code, 2026-10-17): src/evaluate.py eligibility()/availability() apply purge as ~(t + H <= b) at every slice end; isolate_test_labels() blanks every y with t + H > test start before M3; D-022/D-023 fix 'a training row with t + H = cut-off is kept'; tests/test_evaluate.py and tests/test_run_all.py assert purge counts (0 at H = 1; 2 x 24 = 48 rows per cut-off at H = 3, rows C-2h and C-1h); the rolling recent-rate baseline uses s in [t - 14d, t - H] (label maturity, D-021/D-025), which is purging applied online; the M7 weekly refit (scripts/run_improve.py refit_windows) fits on [start, C - 14d) with t + H <= C - 14d, early-stops on [C - 14d, C) with t + H <= C, and scores [C, next cut-off) only, so it purges at both inner cut-offs. Not needed in the project: an embargo, because no split ever trains on data after its scored block. Feature-side leakage is covered separately by the truncation test with a negative control (tests/test_leakage.py).
test_window_hygiene: Lopez de Prado's main warning is backtest overfitting: repeated trials on the same test path inflate apparent skill, so the number of trials should be recorded and the test should not guide model choice. Our analogues: D-021 'score the final test once', the code fingerprint pre-registration (D-028) and the run_all guard that refuses refits after the test marker exists; M7 post-hoc variants were pre-declared and are labelled post-hoc next to the frozen headline (proposed D-030), which is the honest reporting Lopez de Prado recommends.
headline_results: (1) Bergmeir & Benitez 2012: in an empirical comparison of six model-selection procedures (CV-based and last-block hold-out) over four ML/regression techniques on synthetic and real series, the theoretical flaws of CV for time series had no observed practical consequences, and CV gave more robust model selection; they recommend blocked CV as the standard. The study is limited to stationary settings. (2) Bergmeir, Hyndman & Koo 2018: for purely autoregressive models with uncorrelated errors, standard K-fold CV is valid and performs favourably vs OOS evaluation and non-dependent CV; with residual autocorrelation (underfitting) CV underestimates error. A 2025 arXiv note argues CV is biased in general even with MDS residuals [uncertain: not reviewed in depth]. (3) Cerqueira et al. 2020 (174 real series + 3 synthetic): blocked CV is reasonable for stationary series; for non-stationary real-world series the most accurate estimates come from out-of-sample methods that preserve temporal order, particularly hold-out repeated over multiple test periods. (4) Lopez de Prado 2018: standard K-fold overstates performance in finance because labels overlap and features are serially correlated; purged K-fold + embargo removes this leakage; CPCV produces many backtest paths (C(N-1, k-1)) instead of one. No controlled numeric benchmark is reported in the book [uncertain]. (5) Hewamalage et al. 2023: leakage can make a random walk appear to beat the naive benchmark; rolling-origin preferred under non-stationarity. (6) Tashman 2000: rolling-origin evaluation with multiple test periods gives more reliable accuracy estimates than a single fixed origin.
code_available: Not applicable for the papers (no code for Bergmeir & Benitez 2012). Implementations: R forecast::CVar (K-fold CV for AR models with Ljung-Box check); scikit-learn TimeSeriesSplit(gap, test_size, max_train_size), BSD-3; Lopez de Prado-style PurgedKFold / CPCV in temporalcv, skfolio, mizarlabs, fynance (mlfinlab went closed-source). No new dependency is needed for this project: purge and maturity rules are already a few lines in src/evaluate.py, src/baselines.py and scripts/run_improve.py.
takeaways_for_project:
1) Our purge rule is exactly Lopez de Prado purging specialised to forward-only splits: keep a training/early-stopping row iff t + H <= cut-off (D-022, D-023, ratified for D-014 in M8). Write it in the README in these terms and cite Lopez de Prado 2018 ch. 7. State plainly that at H = 1 on an hourly grid the purge removes 0 rows (labels (t, t+1] end at or before the cut-off), and that it binds at H = 3 (48 rows per cut-off), which the tests already pin. Keep those tests; they are the guard if H changes.
2) No embargo is needed and none should be claimed: no split in M3/M4/M7 trains on data after its scored block (train < validation < test; weekly refit fits only before C). Document why (embargo protects training data that FOLLOWS a test fold). If anyone proposes blocked or K-fold CV over the whole history, embargo would become necessary AND would still not fix regime leakage.
3) Do not adopt K-fold or blocked CV for this project. Bergmeir et al. 2018's validity conditions (stationary, purely autoregressive, uncorrelated residuals) fail: we have calendar and spatial features, a measured base-rate shift (train 0.0903 vs validation 0.1179, D-025), and known regime breaks (Jan-2025 drone surge, 2025 raion reform, Sep-2026 reform). Cerqueira et al. 2020 show forward-only, repeated hold-out is the most accurate estimator on non-stationary real data, which supports our walk-forward-by-date design (CLAUDE.md Evaluation) and the M7 inner rolling folds.
4) Split by DATE across all 24 units at once (CLAUDE.md). Never use sklearn TimeSeriesSplit on the stacked panel by row index: gap counts rows, not hours, and a row cut inside an hour separates same-hour oblasts that are strongly correlated during mass attacks (cross-sectional leakage, Roberts et al. 2017).
5) Label maturity is purging done online. Every rolling statistic built from labels (recent-rate baseline D-021/D-025, M7 offset and 14/30-day rate features, proposed D-030) must use s <= t - H. Keep the existing test (tests/test_baselines.py::test_recent_rate_label_maturity) and add the same check for any new label-derived feature.
6) Purging handles labels only. Feature look-back across a cut-off is legitimate (known at t); feature look-AHEAD is not fixed by any split, so the truncation test with its negative control (tests/test_leakage.py) remains the main leakage proof (D-023).
7) Embargo-like exclusions already exist for a different reason: the 24h post-gap mask (D-022) and NaN features after the gap (D-024) exclude rows whose state or inputs are unknowable, not rows that leak. Apply the same logic to the new-regime API window (D-015): the dump starts at 2026-09-12 17:16 UTC after a 7-12 Sep hole, so state is unknowable for the first 24h (D-020 cap) and 7-day look-back features are incomplete for the first 7 days; mask or NaN them and print the count, as D-024 does [recommendation; not checked against the M4 new-regime code].
8) Weekly refit (D-014): the current design (fit [start, C - 14d) with t + H <= C - 14d; early stopping [C - 14d, C) with t + H <= C; score [C, next C)) purges correctly at both inner cut-offs and respects 'no refit on train+val after early stopping' (D-021). Note in the README that each step therefore never trains on its most recent 14 days.
9) Uncertainty of the gain (D-013): use week blocks spanning all 24 units; if H > 1 is ever reported, note that overlapping labels reduce the effective sample size (Lopez de Prado's uniqueness argument), so row-level iid tests would be overconfident.
10) Backtest overfitting: the M7 post-hoc variants on the seen test are a multiple-trial situation (Lopez de Prado; Bailey et al. on PBO). Keep the pre-declared list, report every variant and the number tried, and keep the frozen headline (D-021, D-028); a clean estimate of any M7 winner needs new post-reform data.
best_practices: ADOPT: (a) Forward-only, date-based walk-forward evaluation with all panel units in the same block (Tashman; Cerqueira et al.). (b) Purge at every cut-off with the rule t + H <= cut-off, applied to training AND early-stopping AND calibration slices, and report the purge count per cut-off (Lopez de Prado). (c) Label maturity (s <= t - H) for every rolling label-derived statistic. (d) Inner rolling-origin folds for model/feature selection, identical rows per candidate, all before validation. (e) A pre-registered, once-only final test and a recorded count of trials (anti-backtest-overfitting). (f) Separate tests for label leakage (purge counts) and feature leakage (truncation test with negative control). (g) Block bootstrap over time blocks for CIs; account for label overlap when H > 1. (h) Check residual autocorrelation (Ljung-Box) before ever trusting K-fold CV on a time series. AVOID: (1) Random K-fold or shuffled splits on time-series rows. (2) Blocked K-fold that trains on data after the test block for non-stationary series, even with purge+embargo, because it leaks the future regime level. (3) Row-index splits or row-count gaps on a stacked panel (sklearn TimeSeriesSplit default use). (4) Claiming 'purged' when H = 1 makes the purge a no-op, or omitting the purge when H > 1. (5) Fitting scalers, encoders, calibration maps or rate priors on data that includes the scored period. (6) Treating embargo as a fix for feature look-ahead. (7) Reporting the best of many variants tried on the same test path without disclosing the number of trials.
